sm: Two economists, who both spent time in Europe this summer, ask whether Europe is doomed or just badly behind. One speaker says Europe has fallen far behind, with median income in the United States perhaps thirty or forty percent higher, and rejects the argument that the gap is only about technology. They joke about the lack of air conditioning in Paris during a heat wave, and note that homes in a far-right stronghold in France did have it, which they take as a sign of how people see progress. They criticize Europe's climate focus as costly to growth and partly performative when China, India and the United States are not following, and they note that Europe's energy policy has made it dependent on foreign fuel. They also discuss Germany shutting down nuclear power, and a World Economic Forum moment when European leaders looked alarmed at a pledge to double American electricity output for AI.

The speakers separate two questions: whether Europe has fallen behind, and whether that will last forever. One recalls that Germany was called the sick man of Europe after reunification, then recovered, and could do so again. The other argues Germany's manufacturing-led comeback left it vulnerable, because it did not build a culture of entrepreneurship that could embrace new technology. They say Europe's top need is a Europe-wide bankruptcy law so firms can raise money across borders, and that the European Central Bank says this is coming. They discuss how the euro project wants the benefits of scale without real integration, with national bonds that are partly guaranteed, and an International Monetary Fund finding of tariff-like barriers between European states. They also argue that Europe must let Germany build up militarily, since France is cautious about German strength.

The conversation turns to military integration, with one speaker saying Europe cannot keep separate national generals and needs an integrated command. They say pressure from Russia, migration from Africa and Greenland tensions with the United States could push Europe toward unity. They call the creation of the euro an incredible technical achievement and say similar steps are needed for bankruptcy law and defense. They discuss the dollar's dominance in payment systems, and Canada drawing closer to Europe through a trade deal. One speaker warns the United States faces risks too, including AI and a possible stock market collapse, and a constitutional crisis. They note that Europe as a union is young, dating to the Maastricht Treaty, and then swap a story about being sent to sit in a basement closet at the OECD in Paris after criticizing a paper.

The speakers recall Paris and France, including a senior official in 2009 claiming the financial crisis proved Europe's slow, steady model was better. One speaker remembers European bankers at the Bank of France cheerfully watching American troubles in 2008, not realizing the crisis would hit them as well. They say Americans should be humble, since many social features that hold Europe back are missing in the United States and there is a hunger for them, such as European-style health care. They argue Europeans are more risk-averse and wonder whether they can afford that with an aging population, and they discuss whether regulation should be cut as the Draghi report urges. They say Europe's institutions are under less strain than America's, the far right is rising, and the euro is more likely than not to last twenty years, though unanimity rules make it hard to govern.

The speakers discuss whether Europe can revive its economy without embracing risk and new technology. One argues defense technology like drones, as seen in Ukraine's startups, does not need giant spending, so Germany or Europe could be competitive. They cite a paper suggesting American hours worked per person among prime-age adults are now close to European levels, because so many Americans are out of the labor force. They talk about France's thirty-five hour week, weekend email rules, and a French couple discussing a data center deal on a Saturday. They note that Europeans are good at leisure and keep lifelong friends, while Americans are mobile and economically efficient. They suggest Europe may be ahead of the curve if AI reduces jobs, citing Norwegians working fewer hours and Europe's success in sports.

In the closing section, the speakers say Americans who want to work in Europe tend to be less happy, but Europe has natural advantages and these things move in long cycles. They discuss the strong dollar, which exaggerates the value of the US stock market and GDP relative to Europe, and say Europe is cheap for Americans on American salaries. They add that the suburbs of France can be rough, unlike American suburbs. Both stress how far Europe has come, recalling when Italy, Spain and Portugal were very poor, and when landlines, refrigeration and central heating were rare in Britain. They say Europe adopted broadband quickly after skipping dial-up, so it is not an early adopter but waits until technology is tested. They end by saying their criticism comes from love for Europe, which has great potential, and that they will revisit the topic in a couple of years.
